Main.sentence: Human spaceflight (also referred to as crewed spaceflight , or more historically manned spaceflight ) is ___E:spaceflight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight)___ with a crew or passengers aboard a ___E:spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft)___ , often with the spacecraft being operated directly by the onboard human crew. Spacecraft can also be ___E:remotely operated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telerobotic)___ from ground stations on Earth, or ___E:autonomously U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_robot)___ , without any direct human involvement.

People trained for spaceflight are called ___E:astronauts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut)___ (American or other), cosmonauts (Russian), or taikonauts (Chinese); and non-professionals are referred to as ___E:spaceflight participants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight_participant)___ or spacefarers .

The first human in space was ___E:Soviet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ cosmonaut ___E:Yuri Gagarin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin)___ , who launched as part of the Soviet Union's ___E:Vostok program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_program)___ on ___E:12 April 1961 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmonautics_Day)___ at the beginning of the ___E:Space Race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race)___ .

On 5 May 1961, ___E:Alan Shepard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shepard)___ became the first American in space, as part of ___E:Project Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury)___ .

Humans traveled to ___E:the Moon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moon)___ nine times between 1968 and 1972 as part of the United States' ___E:Apollo program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program)___ , and have had a continuous presence in space for 24 years and 351 days on the ___E:International Space Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station)___ (ISS).

On 15 October 2003, the first Chinese taikonaut, ___E:Yang Liwei U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Liwei)___ , went to space as part of ___E:Shenzhou 5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhou_5)___ , the first Chinese human spaceflight.

As of March 2025, humans have not traveled beyond ___E:low Earth orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit)___ since the ___E:Apollo 17 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_17)___ ___E:lunar mission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_missions_to_the_Moon)___ in December 1972.

Currently, the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ , Russia, and China are the only countries with ___E:public or commercial human spaceflight-capable programs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight_programs)___ . ___E:Non-governmental spaceflight companies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_private_spaceflight_companies)___ have been working to develop human space programs of their own, e.g. for ___E:space tourism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tourism)___ or commercial ___E:in-space research U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_research)___ .

The first private human spaceflight launch was a ___E:suborbital flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suborbital_flight)___ on ___E:SpaceShipOne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceShipOne)___ on June 21, 2004. The first commercial ___E:orbital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_spaceflight)___ crew launch was by ___E:SpaceX U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX)___ in May 2020, transporting ___E:NASA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA)___ astronauts to the ___E:ISS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS)___ under United States government contract.
Human spaceflight capability was first developed during the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ between the United States and the Soviet Union (USSR).

These nations developed ___E:intercontinental ballistic missiles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile)___ for the delivery of ___E:nuclear weapons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon)___ , producing rockets large enough to be adapted to carry the first ___E:artificial satellites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_satellite)___ into ___E:low Earth orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit)___ .

After the first satellites were launched in 1957 and 1958 by the Soviet Union, the US began work on ___E:Project Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury)___ , with the aim of launching men into orbit.

The USSR was pursuing the ___E:Vostok program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_programme)___ to accomplish the same thing, and launched the first human into space, the cosmonaut ___E:Yuri Gagarin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin)___ .

On 12 April 1961, Gagarin was launched aboard ___E:Vostok 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1)___ on a ___E:Vostok 3KA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_3KA)___ rocket and completed a orbit.

On 5 May 1961, the US launched its first ___E:astronaut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut)___ , ___E:Alan Shepard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shepard)___ , on a suborbital flight aboard Freedom 7 on a ___E:Mercury-Redstone rocket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury-Redstone_Launch_Vehicle)___ .

On 20 February 1962, ___E:John Glenn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn)___ became the first American in orbit, aboard Friendship 7 on a ___E:Mercury-Atlas rocket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_LV-3B)___ .

The USSR launched five more cosmonauts in Vostok ___E:capsules U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_capsule)___ , including the first woman in space, ___E:Valentina Tereshkova U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentina_Tereshkova)___ , aboard ___E:Vostok 6 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_6)___ on 16 June 1963. Through 1963, the US launched a total of two astronauts in suborbital flights and four into orbit.

The US also made two ___E:North American X-15 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_X-15)___ flights ( ___E:90 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-15_Flight_90)___ and ___E:91 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-15_Flight_91)___ , piloted by ___E:Joseph A. Walker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_A._Walker)___ ), that exceeded the ___E:Kármán line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A1rm%C3%A1n_line)___ , the 100 kilometres (62 mi) altitude used by the ___E:Fédération Aéronautique Internationale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_A%C3%A9ronautique_Internationale)___ (FAI) to denote the edge of space.

In 1961, US President ___E:John F. Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy)___ raised the stakes of the Space Race by setting the goal of landing a man on the ___E:Moon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon)___ and returning him safely to Earth by the end of the 1960s.

That same year, the US began the ___E:Apollo program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program)___ of launching three-man capsules atop the ___E:Saturn family of launch vehicles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_(rocket_family))___ .

In 1962, the US began ___E:Project Gemini U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini)___ , which flew 10 missions with two-man crews launched by ___E:Titan II rockets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_II_GLV)___ in 1965 and 1966. Gemini's objective was to support Apollo by developing American orbital spaceflight experience and techniques to be used during the Moon mission.

Meanwhile, the USSR intentions to send humans to the Moon and proceeded to stretch the limits of their single-pilot Vostok capsule by adapting it to a two or three-person ___E:Voskhod U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voskhod_programme)___ capsule to compete with Gemini.

They were able to launch two orbital flights in 1964 and 1965 and achieved the first ___E:spacewalk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk)___ , performed by ___E:Alexei Leonov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Leonov)___ on ___E:Voskhod 2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voskhod_2)___ , on 8 March 1965. The US succeeded in developing the ___E:Saturn V U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V)___ rocket necessary to send the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon, and sent ___E:Frank Borman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Borman)___ , ___E:James Lovell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Lovell)___ , and ___E:William Anders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Anders)___ into 10 orbits around the Moon in ___E:Apollo 8 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_8)___ in December 1968. In 1969, ___E:Apollo 11 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11)___ accomplished Kennedy's goal by landing ___E:Neil Armstrong U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Armstrong)___ and ___E:Buzz Aldrin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzz_Aldrin)___ on the Moon on 21 July and returning them safely on 24 July, along with Command Module pilot ___E:Michael Collins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Collins_(astronaut))___ .

Through 1972, a total of six Apollo missions landed 12 men to walk on the Moon, half of which drove ___E:electric powered vehicles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Roving_Vehicle)___ on the surface.

The crew of ___E:Apollo 13 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13)___ — ___E:Jim Lovell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Lovell)___ , ___E:Jack Swigert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Swigert)___ , and ___E:Fred Haise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Haise)___ —survived an in-flight spacecraft failure, they flew by the Moon without landing, and returned safely to Earth.
During this time, the USSR ___E:crewed lunar orbiting and landing programs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_crewed_lunar_programs)___ .

They successfully developed the three-person ___E:Soyuz spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft)___ for use in the lunar programs, but failed to develop the ___E:N1 rocket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N1_(rocket))___ necessary for a human landing, and discontinued their lunar programs in 1974.  Upon losing the Moon race they concentrated on the development of ___E:space stations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station)___ , using the Soyuz as a ferry to take cosmonauts to and from the stations.
They started with a series of ___E:Salyut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_program)___ sortie stations from 1971 to 1986.

In 1969, Nixon appointed his vice president, ___E:Spiro Agnew U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiro_Agnew)___ , to head a Space Task Group to recommend follow-on human spaceflight programs after Apollo.

The group proposed an ambitious ___E:Space Transportation System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Transportation_System)___ based on a ___E:reusable Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_design_process)___ , which consisted of a winged, internally fueled orbiter stage burning liquid hydrogen, launched with a similar, but larger ___E:kerosene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RP-1)___ -fueled booster stage, each equipped with airbreathing jet engines for powered return to a runway at the ___E:Kennedy Space Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center)___ launch site. Other components of the system included a permanent, modular space station; reusable ___E:space tug U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tug)___ ; and ___E:nuclear U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NERVA)___ interplanetary ferry, leading to a ___E:human expedition to Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_mission_to_Mars)___ as early as 1986 or as late as 2000, depending on the level of funding allocated.

However, Nixon knew the American political climate would not support congressional funding for such an ambition, and killed proposals for all but the Shuttle, possibly to be followed by the space station. ___E:Plans for the Shuttle were scaled back U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ to reduce development risk, cost, and time, replacing the piloted fly-back booster with two reusable ___E:solid rocket boosters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster)___ , and the smaller orbiter would use an expendable ___E:external propellant tank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank)___ to feed its hydrogen-fueled ___E:main engines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_main_engine)___ .
The orbiter would have to make unpowered landings.
In 1973, the US launched the ___E:Skylab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylab)___ sortie space station and inhabited it for 171 days with three crews ferried aboard an Apollo spacecraft.

During that time, President ___E:Richard Nixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon)___ and Soviet general secretary ___E:Leonid Brezhnev U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Brezhnev)___ were negotiating an easing of Cold War tensions known as ___E:détente U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente)___ .

During the détente, they negotiated the ___E:Apollo–Soyuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo%E2%80%93Soyuz)___ program, in which an Apollo spacecraft carrying a special docking adapter module would rendezvous and dock with ___E:Soyuz 19 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_19)___ in 1975. The American and Soviet crews shook hands in space.
US turned to developing the Space Shuttle and planning the space station, which was dubbed Freedom .
The USSR launched three ___E:Almaz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz)___ military sortie stations from 1973 to 1977, disguised as Salyuts.

They followed Salyut with the development of Mir , the first modular, semi-permanent space station, the construction of which took place from 1986 to 1996. Mir orbited at an altitude of 354 kilometers (191 nautical miles), at an ___E:orbital inclination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination)___ of 51.6°.
It was occupied for 4,592 days and made a controlled reentry in 2001.
The Space Shuttle started flying in 1981, but the US Congress failed to approve sufficient funds to make Space Station Freedom a reality.
A fleet of four shuttles was built: Columbia , Challenger , Discovery , and Atlantis .

A fifth shuttle, Endeavour , was built to replace Challenger , which was destroyed in ___E:an accident during launch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster)___ that killed 7 astronauts on 28 January 1986. From 1983 to 1998, twenty-two Shuttle flights carried components for a ___E:European Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ sortie space station called ___E:Spacelab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab)___ in the Shuttle payload bay.

The USSR called Buran -class orbiter or simply Buran , which was designed to be launched into orbit by the expendable ___E:Energia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energia_(rocket))___ rocket, and was capable of robotic orbital flight and landing.
Unlike the Space Shuttle, Buran had no main rocket engines, but like the Space Shuttle orbiter, it used smaller rocket engines to perform its final orbital insertion.

A single uncrewed orbital test flight took place in November 1988. A second test flight was planned by 1993, but the program was canceled due to lack of funding and the ___E:dissolution of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ in 1991. Two more orbiters were never completed, and the one that performed the uncrewed flight was destroyed in a hangar roof collapse in May 2002.

The Soviet Soyuz and Mir programs were taken over by the Russian Federal Space Agency, which became known as the ___E:Roscosmos State Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos_State_Corporation)___ .

The ___E:Shuttle-Mir Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Mir_Program)___ included American Space Shuttles visiting the Mir space station, Russian cosmonauts flying on the Shuttle, and an American astronaut flying aboard a Soyuz spacecraft for long-duration expeditions aboard Mir .

In 1993, President ___E:Bill Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton)___ secured Russia's cooperation in converting the planned Space Station Freedom into the ___E:International Space Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station)___ (ISS).
Construction of the station began in 1998. The station orbits at an altitude of 409 kilometers (221 nmi) and an orbital inclination of 51.65°.

Several of the Space Shuttle's 135 orbital flights were to help assemble, supply, and crew the ISS. Russia has built half of the International Space Station and has continued its cooperation with the US.
China was the third nation in the world, after the USSR and US, to send humans into space.

During the ___E:Space Race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race)___ between the two superpowers, which culminated with ___E:Apollo 11 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11)___ landing humans on the Moon, ___E:Mao Zedong U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong)___ and ___E:Zhou Enlai U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai)___ decided on 14 July 1967 that China should not be left behind, and initiated their own crewed space program: the top-secret Project 714, which aimed to put two people into space by 1973 with the ___E:Shuguang U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuguang_spacecraft)___ spacecraft.

Nineteen ___E:PLAAF U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLAAF)___ pilots were selected for this goal in March 1971. The Shuguang-1 spacecraft, to be launched with the ___E:CZ-2A U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ-2A)___ rocket, was designed to carry a crew of two. The program was officially canceled on 13 May 1972 for economic reasons.

In 1992, under ___E:China Manned Space Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Manned_Space_Program)___ (CMS), also known as "Project 921", authorization and funding was given for the first phase of a third, successful attempt at crewed spaceflight.

To achieve independent human spaceflight capability, China developed the ___E:Shenzhou spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhou_spacecraft)___ and ___E:Long March 2F U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_March_2F)___ rocket dedicated to human spaceflight in the next few years, along with critical infrastructures like a new launch site and flight control center being built.
The first uncrewed spacecraft, Shenzhou 1 , was launched on 20 November 1999 and recovered the next day, marking the first step of the realization of China's human spaceflight capability.
Three more uncrewed missions were conducted in the next few years in order to verify the key technologies.

On 15 October 2003 Shenzhou 5 , China's first crewed spaceflight mission, put Yang Liwei in orbit for 21 hours and returned safely back to ___E:Inner Mongolia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Mongolia)___ , making China the third nation to launch a human into orbit independently.

The goal of the second phase of CMS was to make technology breakthroughs in ___E:extravehicular activities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activities)___ (EVA, or spacewalk), ___E:space rendezvous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rendezvous)___ , and ___E:docking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docking_and_berthing_of_spacecraft)___ to support short-term human activities in space.

On 25 September 2008 during the flight of Shenzhou 7 , Zhai Zhigang and Liu Boming completed China's first EVA.  In 2011, China launched the ___E:Tiangong 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiangong_1)___ target spacecraft and Shenzhou 8 uncrewed spacecraft.

The two spacecraft completed China's first automatic rendezvous and docking on 3 November 2011.  About 9 months later, Tiangong 1 completed the first manual rendezvous and docking with Shenzhou 9 , which carried China's first female astronaut Liu Yang .
In September 2016, Tiangong 2 was launched into orbit.
It was a space laboratory with more advanced functions and equipment than Tiangong 1 .
A month later, Shenzhou 11 was launched and docked with Tiangong 2 .
Two astronauts entered Tiangong 2 and were stationed for about 30 days, verifying the viability of astronauts' medium-term stay in space.

In April 2017, China's first cargo spacecraft, Tianzhou 1 docked with Tiangong 2 and completed multiple in-orbit propellant refueling tests, which marked the successful completion of the second phase of CMS.
The third phase of CMS began in 2020. The goal of this phase is to build China's own space station, ___E:Tiangong U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiangong_Space_Station)___ .

The first module of Tiangong , the ___E:Tianhe core module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tianhe_core_module)___ , was launched into orbit by China's most powerful rocket ___E:Long March 5B U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_March_5B)___ on 29 April 2021.  It was later visited by multiple cargo and crewed spacecraft and demonstrated China's capability of sustaining Chinese astronauts' long-term stay in space.

According to CMS announcement, all missions of Tiangong Space Station are scheduled to be carried out by the end of 2022.  Once the construction is completed, Tiangong will enter the application and development phase, which is poised to last for no less than 10 years.

The ___E:European Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ began development of the ___E:Hermes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermes_(spacecraft))___ shuttle ___E:spaceplane U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane)___ in 1987, to be launched on the ___E:Ariane 5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariane_5)___ expendable launch vehicle.
It was intended to dock with the European ___E:Columbus space station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Man-Tended_Free_Flyer)___ .
The projects were canceled in 1992 when it became clear that neither cost nor performance goals could be achieved.
No Hermes shuttles were ever built.
The Columbus space station was reconfigured as the ___E:European module of the same name U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_(ISS_module))___ on the International Space Station.

Japan ( ___E:NASDA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASDA)___ ) began the development of the ___E:HOPE-X U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOPE-X)___ experimental shuttle spaceplane in the 1980s, to be launched on its ___E:H-IIA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-IIA)___ expendable launch vehicle.

A string of failures in 1998 led to funding reductions, and the project's cancellation in 2003 in favor of participation in the International Space Station program through the ___E:Kibō Japanese Experiment Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibo_(ISS_module))___ and ___E:H-II Transfer Vehicle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-II_Transfer_Vehicle)___ cargo spacecraft.

As an alternative to HOPE-X, NASDA in 2001 proposed the ___E:Fuji crew capsule U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuji_(spacecraft))___ for independent or ISS flights, but the project did not proceed to the contracting stage. [citation needed]

From 1993 to 1997, the ___E:Japanese Rocket Society U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japanese_Rocket_Society&action=edit&redlink=1)___ [ja] , ___E:Kawasaki Heavy Industries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawasaki_Heavy_Industries)___ , and ___E:Mitsubishi Heavy Industries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi_Heavy_Industries)___ worked on the proposed ___E:Kankoh-maru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kankoh-maru)___ ___E:vertical-takeoff-and-landing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_takeoff_and_landing)___ ___E:single-stage-to-orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-stage-to-orbit)___ reusable launch system.
In 2005, this system was proposed for space tourism.

According to a press release from the ___E:Iraqi News Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_News_Agency)___ dated 5 December 1989, there was only one test of the ___E:Al-Abid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Abid)___ space launcher, which ___E:Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq)___ intended to use to develop its own crewed space facilities by the end of the century.
These plans were put to an end by the ___E:Gulf War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War)___ of 1991 and the economic hardships that followed.

Under the George W. Bush administration, the ___E:Constellation program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_program)___ included plans for retiring the Space Shuttle program and replacing it with the capability for spaceflight beyond low Earth orbit.

In the ___E:2011 United States federal budget U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_United_States_federal_budget)___ , the Obama administration canceled Constellation for being over budget and behind schedule, while not innovating and investing in critical new technologies.

As part of the ___E:Artemis program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program)___ , NASA is developing the ___E:Orion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(spacecraft))___ spacecraft to be launched by the ___E:Space Launch System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Launch_System)___ .

Under the ___E:Commercial Crew Development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Crew_Development)___ plan, NASA relies on transportation services provided by the private sector to reach low Earth orbit, such as ___E:SpaceX Dragon 2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Dragon_2)___ , the ___E:Boeing Starliner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner)___ or ___E:Sierra Nevada Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_Corporation)___ 's ___E:Dream Chaser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Chaser)___ .

The period between the retirement of the Space Shuttle in 2011 and the first launch into space of ___E:SpaceShipTwo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceShipTwo)___ ___E:Flight VP-03 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VSS_Unity_VP-03)___ on 13 December 2018 is similar to the gap between the end of ___E:Apollo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program)___ in 1975 and the ___E:first Space Shuttle flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1)___ in 1981, and is referred to by a presidential Blue Ribbon Committee as the U.S. human spaceflight gap.
Since the early 2000s, a variety of ___E:private spaceflight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_spaceflight)___ ventures have been undertaken.

As of November 2024, [update] ___E:SpaceX U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX)___  and ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___  have launched humans to orbit, [note 1] while ___E:Blue Origin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Origin)___ has launched 8 crewed flights, six of which crossed the ___E:Kármán line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A1rm%C3%A1n_line)___ .  [note 2] ___E:Virgin Galactic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Galactic)___ has launched crew to a height above 80 km (50 mi) on a suborbital trajectory.

Several other companies, including ___E:Sierra Nevada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Nevada_Corporation)___ and ___E:Copenhagen Suborbitals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_Suborbitals)___ , have developed crewed spacecraft.
SpaceX, Boeing, Blue Origin, and Virgin Galactic plan to fly commercial passengers in the emerging ___E:space tourism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_tourism)___ market.

___E:SpaceX U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX)___ has developed ___E:Crew Dragon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Dragon)___ flying on ___E:Falcon 9 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_9)___ .
It first launched astronauts to orbit and to the ISS in May 2020 as part of the ___E:Demo-2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Dragon_Demo-2)___ mission.
Developed as part of NASA's ___E:Commercial Crew Development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_Crew_Development)___ program, the capsule is also available for flights with other customers.
A first tourist mission, ___E:Inspiration4 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspiration4)___ , launched in September 2021.

Participation and representation of humanity in space has been an issue ever since the first phase of space exploration.

Some rights of non-spacefaring countries have been secured through international ___E:space law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_law)___ , declaring space the " ___E:province of all mankind U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_heritage_of_mankind)___ ", though the sharing of space by all humanity is sometimes criticized as ___E:imperialist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism)___ and lacking.
In addition to the lack of international inclusion, the inclusion of women and ___E:people of color U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_of_color)___ has also been lacking.

The first woman to ever enter space was ___E:Valentina Tereshkova U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentina_Tereshkova)___ .

At the time, all astronauts were required to be military test pilots; women were not able to enter this career, which is one reason for the delay in allowing women to join space crews.

After the rules were changed, ___E:Svetlana Savitskaya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svetlana_Savitskaya)___ became the second woman to enter space; she was also from the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ . ___E:Sally Ride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Ride)___ became the next woman to enter space and the first woman to enter space through the United States program.Since then, eleven other countries have allowed women astronauts.
The first all-female spacewalk occurred in 2018, by ___E:Christina Koch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Koch)___ and ___E:Jessica Meir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Meir)___ .
These two women had both participated in separate spacewalks with NASA. The first mission to the Moon with a woman aboard is planned for 2024.
Despite these developments, women are still underrepresented among astronauts and especially cosmonauts.
More than 600 people have flown in space but only 75 have been women.

There are two main sources of hazard in space flight: those due to the hostile space environment, and those due to possible equipment malfunctions.
Addressing these issues is of great importance for NASA and other space agencies before conducting the first extended crewed missions to destinations such as Mars.
Planners of human spaceflight missions face a number of safety concerns.
The basic needs for breathable air and drinkable water are addressed by the ___E:life support system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support_system)___ of the spacecraft.
Astronauts may not be able to quickly return to Earth or receive medical supplies, equipment, or personnel if a medical emergency occurs.
The astronauts may have to rely for long periods on limited resources and medical advice from the ground.

The possibility of ___E:blindness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blindness)___ and of ___E:bone loss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_Loss)___ have been associated with human ___E:space flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight)___ .

On 31 December 2012, a ___E:NASA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA)___ -supported study reported that spaceflight may harm the brains of ___E:astronauts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronauts)___ and accelerate the onset of ___E:Alzheimer's disease U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alzheimer%27s_disease)___ .

In October 2015, the ___E:NASA Office of Inspector General U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Office_of_Inspector_General)___ issued a ___E:health hazards report U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_of_spaceflight_on_the_human_body)___ related to ___E:space exploration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_exploration)___ , which included the potential hazards of a ___E:human mission to Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_mission_to_Mars)___ .

On 2 November 2017, scientists reported, based on ___E:MRI studies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_resonance_imaging)___ , that significant changes in the position and structure of the brain have been found in astronauts who have taken ___E:trips in space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_of_spaceflight_on_the_human_body)___ .
Astronauts on longer space trips were affected by greater brain changes.

Researchers in 2018 reported, after detecting the presence on the ___E:International Space Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station)___ (ISS) of five Enterobacter bugandensis bacterial strains, none ___E:pathogenic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathogen)___ to humans, that ___E:microorganisms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microorganism)___ on ISS should be carefully monitored to assure a healthy environment for ___E:astronauts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut)___ .

In March 2019, NASA reported that latent ___E:viruses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virus)___ in humans may be activated during space missions, possibly adding more risk to astronauts in future deep-space missions.

On 25 September 2021, ___E:CNN U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN)___ reported that an alarm had sounded during the ___E:Inspiration4 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspiration4)___ Earth-orbital journey on the ___E:SpaceX Dragon 2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Dragon_2)___ .
The alarm signal was found to be associated with an apparent toilet malfunction.

Medical data from astronauts in low Earth orbits for long periods, dating back to the 1970s, show several adverse effects of a microgravity environment: loss of ___E:bone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone)___ density, decreased muscle strength and endurance, postural instability, and reductions in aerobic capacity.
Over time these ___E:deconditioning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deconditioning)___ effects can impair astronauts' performance or increase their risk of injury.

In a weightless environment, astronauts put almost no weight on the back ___E:muscles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle)___ or leg muscles used for standing up, which causes the muscles to weaken and get smaller.
Astronauts can lose up to twenty per cent of their muscle mass on spaceflights lasting five to eleven days. The consequent loss of strength could be a serious problem in case of a landing emergency.

Upon returning to Earth from ___E:long-duration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-duration_spaceflight)___ flights, astronauts are considerably weakened and are not allowed to drive a car for twenty-one days.

Astronauts experiencing weightlessness will often lose their orientation, get ___E:motion sickness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_sickness)___ , and lose their sense of direction as their bodies try to get used to a weightless environment.
When they get back to Earth, they have to readjust and may have problems standing up, focusing their gaze, walking, and turning.
Importantly, those motor disturbances only get worse the longer the exposure to weightlessness.
These changes can affect the ability to perform tasks required for approach and landing, docking, remote manipulation, and emergencies that may occur while landing.

In addition, after long ___E:space flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight)___ missions, male astronauts may experience severe ___E:eyesight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_system)___ problems, which may be a major concern for future deep space flight missions, including a ___E:crewed mission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crewed_mission)___ to the planet ___E:Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars)___ .
Long space flights can also alter a space traveler's eye movements.

Without proper shielding, the crews of missions beyond low Earth orbit might be at risk from high-energy protons emitted by ___E:solar particle events U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_particle_event)___ (SPEs) associated with ___E:solar flares U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_flare)___ .

If estimated correctly, the amount of radiation that astronauts would be exposed to from a solar storm similar to that of the most powerful in recorded history, the ___E:Carrington Event U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrington_Event)___ , would result in ___E:acute radiation sickness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acute_radiation_sickness)___ at least, and could even be fatal "in a poorly shielded spacecraft".  [better source needed] Another storm that could have inflicted a potentially lethal dose of radiation on astronauts outside Earth's protective ___E:magnetosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetosphere)___ occurred during the ___E:Space Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Age)___ , shortly after ___E:Apollo 16 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_16)___ landed and before ___E:Apollo 17 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_17)___ launched.

This solar storm, ___E:which occurred in August 1972 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_1972_solar_storm)___ , could potentially have caused any astronauts who were exposed to it to suffer from acute radiation sickness, and may even have been lethal for those engaged in ___E:extravehicular activity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity)___ or on the lunar surface.
Another type of radiation, galactic ___E:cosmic rays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray)___ , presents further challenges to human spaceflight beyond low Earth orbit.

There is also some scientific concern that extended spaceflight might slow down the body's ability to protect itself against diseases,  resulting in a weakened ___E:immune system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immune_system)___ and the activation of dormant ___E:viruses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virus)___ in the body. ___E:Radiation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation)___ can cause both short- and long-term consequences to the bone marrow stem cells from which blood and immune-system cells are created.
Because the interior of a spacecraft is so small, a weakened immune system and more active viruses in the body can lead to a fast spread of infection.

During long missions, astronauts are isolated and confined in small spaces. ___E:Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood))___ , anxiety, ___E:cabin fever U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabin_fever)___ , and other psychological problems may occur more than for an average person and could impact the crew's safety and mission success.
NASA spends millions of dollars on psychological treatments for astronauts and former astronauts.
To date, there is no way to prevent or reduce mental problems caused by extended periods of stay in space.
Due to these mental disorders, the efficiency of astronauts' work is impaired; and sometimes they are brought back to Earth, incurring the expense of their mission being aborted.

A Russian expedition to space in 1976 was returned to Earth after the cosmonauts reported a strong odor that resulted in a fear of fluid leakage; but after a thorough investigation, it became clear that there was no leakage or technical malfunction.
It was concluded by NASA that the cosmonauts most likely had ___E:hallucinated the smell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantosmia)___ .
It is possible that the mental health of astronauts can be affected by the changes in the sensory systems while in prolonged space travel.
During astronauts' spaceflight, they are in an extreme environment.
This, and the fact that little change is taking place in the environment, will result in the weakening of sensory input to the astronauts' seven senses.

Space flight requires much higher velocities than ground or air transportation, and consequently requires the use of high ___E:energy density U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_density)___ propellants for launch, and the dissipation of large amounts of energy, usually as heat, for safe reentry through the Earth's atmosphere.

Since rockets have the potential for fire or explosive destruction, ___E:space capsules U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_capsule)___ generally employ some sort of ___E:launch escape system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_escape_system)___ , consisting either of a tower-mounted solid-fuel rocket to quickly carry the capsule away from the ___E:launch vehicle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_vehicle)___ (employed on ___E:Mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury)___ , ___E:Apollo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_(spacecraft))___ , and ___E:Soyuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft)___ , the escape tower being discarded at some point after launch, at a point where an abort can be performed using the spacecraft's engines), or else ___E:ejection seats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat)___ (employed on ___E:Vostok U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_spacecraft)___ and ___E:Gemini U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini)___ ) to carry astronauts out of the capsule and away for individual parachute landings.

Such a launch escape system is not always practical for multiple-crew-member vehicles (particularly ___E:spaceplanes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane)___ ), depending on the location of egress hatch(es).

When the single-hatch Vostok capsule was modified to become the 2 or 3-person ___E:Voskhod U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voskhod_(spacecraft))___ , the single-cosmonaut ejection seat could not be used, and no escape tower system was added.
The two Voskhod flights in 1964 and 1965 avoided launch mishaps.

The ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ carried ejection seats and escape hatches for its pilot and copilot in early flights; but these could not be used for passengers who sat below the flight deck on later flights, and so were discontinued.
There have been only two in-flight launch aborts of a crewed flight.

The first occurred on ___E:Soyuz 18a U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_7K-T_No.39)___ on 5 April 1975. The abort occurred after the launch escape system had been jettisoned when the launch vehicle's spent second stage failed to separate before the third stage ignited and the vehicle strayed off course.
The crew finally managed to separate the spacecraft, firing its engines to pull it away from the errant rocket, and both cosmonauts landed safely.
The second occurred on 11 October 2018 with the launch of ___E:Soyuz MS-10 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-10)___ .
Again, both crew members survived.

In the first use of a launch escape system on the launchpad, before the start of a crewed flight, happened during the planned ___E:Soyuz T-10a U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_7K-ST_No._16L)___ launch on 26 September 1983, which was aborted by a launch vehicle fire 90 seconds before liftoff.
Both cosmonauts aboard landed safely.

The only crew fatality during launch occurred on 28 January 1986, when the ___E:Space Shuttle Challenger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster)___ broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, due to the failure of a ___E:solid rocket booster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Solid_Rocket_Booster)___ seal, which caused the failure of the ___E:external fuel tank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank)___ , resulting in an explosion of the fuel and separation of the boosters.
All seven crew members were killed.
Tasks outside a spacecraft require use of a ___E:space suit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_suit)___ .
Despite the risk of mechanical failures while working in open space, there have been no spacewalk fatalities.
Spacewalking astronauts routinely remain attached to the spacecraft with tethers and sometimes supplementary anchors.

Un-tethered spacewalks were performed on three missions in 1984 using the ___E:Manned Maneuvering Unit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Maneuvering_Unit)___ , and on a flight test in 1994 of the ___E:Simplified Aid For EVA Rescue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Aid_For_EVA_Rescue)___ (SAFER) device.

The single pilot of ___E:Soyuz 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_1)___ , ___E:Vladimir Komarov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Komarov)___ , was killed when his capsule's parachutes failed during an emergency landing on 24 April 1967, causing the capsule to crash.

On 1 February 2003, the crew of seven aboard the Space Shuttle ___E:Columbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia)___ were ___E:killed on reentry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster)___ after completing a ___E:successful mission in space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107)___ .

A wing-leading-edge ___E:reinforced carbon-carbon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_carbon-carbon)___ heat shield had been damaged by a piece of frozen ___E:external tank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank)___ foam insulation that had broken off and struck the wing during launch.
Hot reentry gasses entered and destroyed the wing structure, leading to the breakup of the ___E:orbiter vehicle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter)___ .

There are two basic choices for an artificial atmosphere: either an Earth-like mixture of oxygen and an inert gas such as nitrogen or helium, or pure oxygen, which can be used at lower than standard atmospheric pressure.

A nitrogen–oxygen mixture is used in the International Space Station and Soyuz spacecraft, while low-pressure pure oxygen is commonly used in space suits for ___E:extravehicular activity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity)___ .

The use of a gas mixture carries the risk of ___E:decompression sickness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decompression_sickness)___ (commonly known as "the bends") when transitioning to or from the pure oxygen space suit environment.
There have been instances of injury and fatalities caused by suffocation in the presence of too much nitrogen and not enough oxygen.
A pure oxygen atmosphere carries the risk of fire. The original design of the Apollo spacecraft used pure oxygen at greater than atmospheric pressure prior to launch.

An electrical fire started in the cabin of ___E:Apollo 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_1)___ during a ground test at ___E:Cape Kennedy Air Force Station Launch Complex 34 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Air_Force_Station_Launch_Complex_34)___ on 27 January 1967, and spread rapidly.

The high pressure, increased by the fire, prevented removal of the ___E:plug door U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plug_door)___ hatch cover in time to rescue the crew. All three astronauts— ___E:Gus Grissom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gus_Grissom)___ , ___E:Ed White U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_White_(astronaut))___ , and ___E:Roger Chaffee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Chaffee)___ —were killed.
This led NASA to use a nitrogen–oxygen atmosphere before launch, and low-pressure pure oxygen only in space.

The March 1966 ___E:Gemini 8 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_8)___ mission was aborted in orbit when an ___E:attitude control system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attitude_control_system)___ thruster stuck in the on position, sending the craft into a dangerous spin that threatened the lives of ___E:Neil Armstrong U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Armstrong)___ and ___E:David Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Scott)___ .
Armstrong had to shut the control system off and use the reentry control system to stop the spin. The craft made an emergency reentry and the astronauts landed safely.

The most probable cause was determined to be an electrical short due to a ___E:static electricity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_electricity)___ discharge, which caused the thruster to remain powered even when switched off. The control system was modified to put each thruster on its own isolated circuit.

The third lunar landing expedition, ___E:Apollo 13 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13)___ , in April 1970, was aborted and the lives of the crew— ___E:James Lovell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Lovell)___ , ___E:Jack Swigert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Swigert)___ , and ___E:Fred Haise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Haise)___ —were threatened after the failure of a ___E:cryogenic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryogenic)___ ___E:liquid oxygen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_oxygen)___ tank en route to the Moon. The tank burst when electrical power was applied to internal stirring fans in the tank, causing the immediate loss of all of its contents, and also damaging the second tank, causing the gradual loss of its remaining oxygen over a period of 130 minutes.

This in turn caused a loss of electrical power provided by ___E:fuel cells U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_cell)___ to the ___E:command spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Command/Service_Module)___ .
The crew managed to return to Earth safely by using the ___E:lunar landing craft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Lunar_Module)___ as a "life boat".

The tank failure was determined to be caused by two mistakes: the tank's drain fitting had been damaged when it was dropped during factory testing, necessitating the use of its internal heaters to boil out the oxygen after a pre-launch test; which in turn damaged the fan wiring's electrical insulation because the thermostats on the heaters did not meet the required voltage rating due to a vendor miscommunication.

The crew of ___E:Soyuz 11 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_11)___ were killed on 30 June 1971 by a combination of mechanical malfunctions; the crew were ___E:asphyxiated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asphyxia)___ due to cabin decompression following the separation of their descent capsule from the service module.

A cabin ventilation valve had been jolted open at an altitude of 168 kilometres (104 mi) by the stronger-than-expected shock of explosive separation bolts, which were designed to fire sequentially, but in fact had fired simultaneously.
The loss of pressure became fatal within about 30 seconds.
As of December 2015 [update] , 23 crew members have died in accidents aboard spacecraft.
Over 100 others have died in accidents during activities directly related to spaceflight or testing.
